content.title: Claryfing the OOD concern of deletion/insertion metrics.
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer kg3f for their thoughtful feedback. We note that the main concern raised is regarding the potential adversarial effect that the removal of input regions can cause the model confidence to drop more than what it should due to the data moving off the natural image manifold. Although relevant, this can be misleading. We hope to clarify this matter in the following. 

The removal of features is performed under certain constraints that are aimed to minimize the adversarial effects. Firstly, the baseline image is a highly-blurred version of the input image (rather than noise, black background, etc.). This avoids introducing sharp edges to the input and causing adversarial effects. In addition, to compute the metrics, the features are not perturbed at the pixel level, rather it is over a patch of neighboring pixels (e.g. 8x8) that also makes adversarial effects more unlikely. 

While we agree to some extent that the deletion metric by itself *can* favor adversarial perturbations, this does not hold for the insertion metric and we mostly make use of the insertion metric in this paper. In order to increase the insertion metric, the network needs to predict high confidence given a small region. Adding the constraint that regions are smooth, It is less likely for adversarial masks to fool this metric because usually off-manifold data results in a drop in the model confidence. In practice, we have observed results to not be of adversarial nature.

Moreover, we aim to analyze the differences in the decision-making mechanism in CNNs and attention models. Random occlusion, despite the OOD concern, is a widely-used exploration tool for this purpose in the literature [1-3]. Instead of using random occlusions, we use occlusions guided by different explanation tools in our study. In addition, usage of the deletion/insertion metrics in the XAI community has been shown to have a direct correlation with non-perturbation-based evaluation metrics [4-6].


[1] Bhojanapalli et al. Understanding robustness of transformers for image classification. ICCV 2021.
[2] Naseer et al. Intriguing Properties of Vision Transformers. NeurIPS 2021.
[3] Paul & Chen.  Vision transformers are robust learners. AAAI 2022.
[4] Wang et al. Score-CAM: Score-Weighted Visual Explanations for Convolutional Neural Networks. CVPRW 2020.
[5] Schulz et al. Restricting the Flow: Information Bottlenecks for Attribution. ICLR 2020.
[6] Qi et al. Visualizing Deep Networks by Optimizing with Integrated Gradients. AAAI 2020.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors want to examine some interesting questions about the differences between CNNs and transformers using deep explanation algorithms. This paper proposed two modality-agnostic methodologies of sub-explanation counting and cross-testing to assess decision-making behaviors. The sub-explanation counting is based on the assumption: the count is higher the explainable regions are more compositional, where the count is calculated by removing the explainable areas from the SAG-based explanations and counting the number of explanations that, after the removal of these areas, can still lead to classification confidences. The cross-testing is based on the assumption: two different recognition models should have similar heatmaps that represent the explainable regions are similar. 
However, the authors didn't provide more evidence to prove the two assumptions are acceptable and in my view, the two assumptions are not strong.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The authors want to examine some interesting questions about the differences between CNNs and transformers using deep explanation algorithms, and proposed two modality-agnostic methodologies of sub-explanation counting and cross-testing to assess decision-making behavior.

Weaknesses:
1. Novelty is somewhat limited. 
2. The assumptions of the proposed methods are not very strong.
3. The paper writing is not very clear, especially regarding the two proposed methods.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a methodology to compare various architecture for image classification tasks (CNN and transformers) using the visual explanations obtained with feature attribution methods (gradient-based and perturbation-based). Two methods are proposed.

The first method is called sub-explanation counting, and uses the concept of Minimal Sufficient Explanation (MSE). It generates MSE subsets, and counts the number of subsets that provide a classification score above given thresholds. The objective is to assess whether partial explanations still retain high classification confidence (compositionality).

The second method is called cross-testing and is used for architecture comparison. It proposes to generate an attribution map from one model, and uses another model to assess the insertion/deletion metrics by successfully masking the image based on the attribution map.

The main results of the paper is to have identified families of architectures based on the statistical and geometric nature of the explanations and to explain the robustness of attention-based architectures compared to convolutional networks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
== Strengths ==
- Interesting work that addresses the quantitative comparison of deep neural network models using statistics of visual explanations, especially the difference between CNN and attention-based architectures.

== Limitations ==
- Findings have a limited scope: they depend on a single heatmap generation (iGOS++), and only address image classification
- Several well studied architectures are missing (e.g. efficientNet).
- It is not clearly proven yet that the explanation differences are due to the architecture differences themselves. For example, they might also be due to the attribution method, and depend on the nature of  classes.
- The comparison between architectures is obtained with statistical explanations, but not individual instances.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Novelty

The idea of exploiting the structure of explanations to compare deep neural network architectures seems to be novel. 

- Clarity & quality

The article is clearly written and easy to follow.

The paper is mostly empirical. The results are interesting, but should be deepened. I agree with the limitations identified by the authors (single heatmap, statistics over dataset, no proven link with architecture), but they are strong limitations and should have been addressed explicitly in the paper.

A few suggestions to broaden the scope of the results:

Regarding convolutional architectures, it would have been interesting to see the differences with parametric architectures such as efficientNet [1]. Is there a correlation between the architecture parameter and the MSE statistics? 

The impact of heatmap generation may be important. For instance,  there exists now a transformer-specific way to compute heatmaps [2] which may behave differently. It would be interesting to see if the results are unchanged.

The literature proposes architectures that combine convolutional + transformers [3-5]: how do they fit in the classification?

An open question. Transformer architectures contain multi-head structures: can it be a cause of what is called “disjunctive behavior” in the paper?

** References:

[1] Tan, M., & Le, Q. (2019, May). Efficientnet: Rethinking model scaling for convolutional neural networks. In International conference on machine learning (pp. 6105-6114). PMLR.

[2] Chefer, H., Gur, S., & Wolf, L. (2021). Transformer interpretability beyond attention visualization. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 782-791)

[3] d’Ascoli, S., Touvron, H., Leavitt, M. L., Morcos, A. S., Biroli, G., & Sagun, L. (2021, July). Convit: Improving vision transformers with soft convolutional inductive biases. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 2286-2296). PMLR.

[4] Guo, J., Han, K., Wu, H., Tang, Y., Chen, X., Wang, Y., & Xu, C. (2022). Cmt: Convolutional neural networks meet vision transformers. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 12175-12185).

[5] Park, N., & Kim, S. (2021, September). How Do Vision Transformers Work?. In International Conference on Learning Representations.

- Reproducibility

Results are obtained with public code (iOGS++),  and public datasets (ImageNet). The code for reproducing experiments is not provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper described an interesting preliminary study but of limited scope, and with results that must be confirmed by supplementary experiments. The limitations, transparently identified by the authors, are strong, and should have been addressed as a main issue.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper compares the minimally-sufficient explanations (MSE) produced by performing a beam search on different patches of the input (here input was limited to images where images were divided into 49 patches) following work done by [1] for different CNNs, global attention models and local attention model. The paper then used two metrics to compare different models (a) sub-explanation counts which are the number of MSE of different networks by first defining the explanations as masks so that the masked images would generate similar predictions as the full image and then systematically removing areas from those explanations and count the number of explanations that, after the removal of these areas, can still lead to classification confidences that are higher than certain thresholds.
(b) Cross testing where the salient regions produced from a single model are tested in other models to determine if it is important for multiple models.
The paper bases its results on intervention experiments that involve masking the salient part of images and checking the effect it has on the class output.
From the proposed metrics the paper concludes that different models exhibit quite different behaviors in their decision-making, local attention models are more likely to exhibit a compositional behavior and global attention models are more likely to exhibit a disjunctive behavior. CNN behaves more similarly to local attention methods than global attention methods.




[1] Vivswan Shitole, Fuxin Li, Minsuk Kahng, Prasad Tadepalli, and Alan Fern. One Explanation is Not Enough: Structured Attention Graphs for Image Classification. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, volume 34, 2021.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The overall idea of understanding how different architecture works and what they focus on is very interesting and understudied I believe this paper touches on a very important area generally having a better understanding of how different architecture work canthe  help AI community build better architecture.


Weakness:

I am afraid that the main premise of this work might be incorrect. The work is based on intervention experiments and these might lead to misleading results. [1] showed that removing features from the input might result in an adversarial effect causing accuracy to drop 
(the same thing should apply to class output and classification confidences) is due to viewing OOD images rather than removing actual salient features. Although the paper did cite this [1] they used deletion and insertion mechanisms throughout the paper. Given this, I am not sure I can trust the results produced by this paper.

Other weakness:
Writing:
- The paper refers to figures and tables in the appendix in the main text (I examined them carefully) however authors should not be using the appendix as an extension of the main text. From the very beginning, the first table referenced (table 3 on page 5) is not in the main text which was a bit confusing.
- In section 4 the paper uses "most experiments" multiple times, this is very confusing because the paper does not specify which experiments were performed as described and which weren't. Nor does it state how other experiments were performed.
- Some parts of the text were not clear and difficult to follow for example section 4.1.
- Graphs in figure 3 were hard to read.





[1] Sara Hooker, Dumitru Erhan, Pieter-Jan Kindermans, and Been Kim. A benchmark for interoperability methods in deep neural networks. Advances in neural information processing systems, 32, 2019.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and Quality -- Poor:
The paper is not well written and difficult to follow.
The paper references the appendix as part of the main text.
The graphs are hard to read.

Novelty--Fair:
The idea of the paper is very good and exciting, however, the execution might be flawed which makes it hard to trust the results provided by the paper.

Reproducibility -- medium:
The paper did mention some experimental details for the different experiments but the code was not provided.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The idea of the paper is great and very important in my opinion. However, to evaluate the different models the paper removed parts of the input and measured change in the score. Removing part of the input can have an adversarial effect on the model since the new input is OOD as discussed by [1]. This makes the analysis and observations produced by the paper questionable. 




[1] Sara Hooker, Dumitru Erhan, Pieter-Jan Kindermans, and Been Kim. A benchmark for interoperability methods in deep neural networks. Advances in neural information processing systems, 32, 2019.

content.title: Examining the Difference Among Transformers and CNNs with Explanation Methods
content.abstract: We propose a methodology that systematically applies deep explanation algorithms on a dataset-wide basis, to compare different types of visual recognition backbones, such as convolutional networks (CNNs), global attention networks, and local attention networks. We examine both qualitative visualizations and quantitative statistics across the dataset, in order to generate intuitions that are not just anecdotal, but are supported by the statistics computed on the whole dataset. Specifically, we propose two methods. The first one, sub-explanation counting, systematically searches for minimally-sufficient explanations of all images and count the amount of sub-explanations for each network. The second one, called cross-testing, computes salient regions using one network and then evaluates the performance by only showing these regions as an image to other networks. Through a combination of qualitative insights and quantitative statistics, we illustrate that 1) there are significant differences between the salient features of CNNs and attention models; 2) the occlusion-robustness in local attention models and global attention models may come from different decision-making mechanisms.
